Contemptible means deserving to be looked down upon with strong moral disgust and disrespect.

When you call something or someone contemptible, you are saying they are so low, dishonest, cowardly, or morally wrong that they earn not just disapproval — but a deep, dismissive scorn. It is a strong word. It does not mean merely "bad." It means shamefully, disgracefully bad.

To fully understand contemptible, you need to understand the noun it comes from: contempt.

Contempt is a specific human feeling — it is the emotion you feel when you look at someone or something and think, "This is beneath me. This is beneath any decent person. This deserves no respect whatsoever."

It is stronger than dislike. It is stronger than disapproval. Contempt carries a sense of moral superiority — the feeling that what you are looking at has failed some basic standard of decency, honesty, or courage so badly that it deserves to be dismissed entirely.

So, contemptible simply means: worthy of that feeling. It describes the thing or person that earns contempt — that deserves to be looked down upon.

Something is contemptible when it shows one or more of these qualities to a degree that shocks our moral sense:

  • Cowardice — A soldier who abandons his fellow soldiers to save himself is contemptible.
  • Dishonesty or betrayal — A person who lies to destroy an innocent person's reputation is contemptible.
  • Cruelty toward the weak — Bullying a child, exploiting an elderly person, or abusing someone who cannot defend themselves is contemptible.
  • Moral smallness — Acting in a petty, self-serving, or utterly spineless way when decency was clearly required.

The common thread is this: contemptible behavior falls below the floor of what we expect from a decent human being. It does not just disappoint us — it disgusts and dishonors us.

His decision to blame his employee for a mistake he made was absolutely contemptible.

The war criminal's attempts to deny his actions in court were contemptible.

She found his cowardice contemptible — he had watched someone get hurt and simply walked away.

Spreading lies about a grieving family to gain attention is a contemptible thing to do.

The politician's contemptible behavior shocked even his own supporters.

Notice that in all these sentences, the word carries weight. It is not used lightly. It signals that the speaker has moved past mere disappointment into moral disgust.

Contemptible is a strong word — use it intentionally.

On a scale of moral disapproval, it sits near the top:

Disappointing → Wrong → Bad → Shameful → Despicable / Contemptible

You would not call someone contemptible for forgetting a birthday or being slightly rude. You use it when someone has done something that reveals a serious failure of character — something cowardly, cruel, dishonest, or deeply unfair.

This is important because learners often confuse related words.

  • Contemptible ≠ Contemptuous

These two words are opposites in direction, and confusing them is a very common mistake.

  • Contemptible = deserving contempt (you are the one being looked down upon)
  • Contemptuous = showing contempt (you are the one doing the looking down)

He gave a contemptuous sneer at the contemptible behavior in front of him.

In that sentence, he is contemptuous (he is expressing scorn), and the behavior is contemptible (it deserves scorn). The person feeling contempt is contemptuous. The thing receiving contempt is contemptible.

  • Contemptible ≠ Pitiful

Something pitiful makes you feel sorry. Something contemptible makes you feel scorn. You pity a sick, helpless animal. You feel contempt toward someone who deliberately and selfishly harms others.

It helps to know the whole family this word belongs to:

  • Contempt (noun) — the feeling of scorn and disgust. "She looked at him with contempt."
  • Contemptible (adjective) — deserving contempt. "His behavior was contemptible."
  • Contemptuous (adjective) — showing or feeling contempt. "She gave a contemptuous look."
  • Contemptuously (adverb) — in a contemptuous manner. "He laughed contemptuously."
  • Contemptibly (adverb) — in a contemptible manner. "He acted contemptibly."
Similar Words — And How They Differ

These words are close in meaning to contemptible, but each has a slightly different flavor:

WordFlavor
DespicableVery similar; emphasizes being worthy of being despised. Often used for cruelty or villainy. "A despicable act of violence."
DeplorableEmphasizes being so bad it deserves strong condemnation; sometimes used for conditions or situations too, not just people. "Deplorable living conditions."
VileEmphasizes extreme disgust, often with a sense of something dirty or morally repulsive. "A vile act of betrayal."
IgnobleEmphasizes a lack of honor or nobility of character; slightly more formal and literary. "An ignoble surrender."
ShamefulEmphasizes that something brings shame, but slightly softer than contemptible.

Of all these, contemptible most specifically means worthy of contempt — deserving to be looked down upon and dismissed with moral disgust.
A Quick Gut-Check to Remember It

Ask yourself this when you see or use the word:

"Does this person or thing deserve to be looked down upon with moral disgust — not just criticized, but genuinely scorned?"

If yes → it is contemptible.

Think of it this way: if a decent, honorable person witnessed the behavior and felt their stomach turn with scorn and shame on behalf of humanity — that behavior is contemptible.
Contemptible describes a person, action, or thing that is so morally low — so cowardly, dishonest, cruel, or disgraceful — that it deserves not just criticism, but deep scorn and dismissal.
